We quantify how quantum effects modify this behavior by tuning the degree of quantumness through variations of the spin quantum number. These findings suggest that quantum synchronization can be enhanced in experiments by harnessing rather than suppressing heterogeneity.

nominations.title: A Universal Approach to Hydrodynamics in Higher Dimensions via Tensor Networks
nominations.authors: Sajant Anand, Christopher D. White, Jack Kemp, Julia Wei, Norman Y. Yao, Michael P. Zaletel
nominations.abstract: Extracting late-time hydrodynamic transport properties directly from microscopic quantum models, especially in dimensions beyond one, is believed to be classically intractable. This owes, in part, to the extensive growth of entanglement in higher dimensions and often a mismatch between geometric and tensor network locality. Here, we extend the Density Matrix Truncation (DMT) algorithm to accurately and quantitatively predict high-temperature transport coefficients (e.g. diffusion constants) in up to three dimensions. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to capture the slow crossover dynamics characteristic of weakly broken integrability. The intuition underlying our approach is to preserve the geometrically local information crucial for hydrodynamics throughout the time evolution, despite using a one-dimensional matrix product state ansatz for higher-dimensional calculations. Our work pushes the boundary of classical computability and opens the door to benchmarking the high-temperature, late-time dynamics of generic quantum simulators.

nominations.title: Fock-space delocalization and its control in scarred-vs-ergodic dynamics
nominations.authors: Francesco Perciavalle
nominations.abstract: Quantum many-body scarred dynamics in Rydberg-atom arrays is characterized by revivals, in which the system repeatedly returns to its initial state despite its many-body complexity. But how extensively does the wave function explore the space of allowed configurations between revivals? We address this question by quantifying the fraction of configurations occupied during PXP dynamics initialized from the paradigmatic polarized and N\'eel states, which respectively exhibit thermalizing and scarred dynamics. Despite their striking revivals, dynamics from the N\'eel state spreads over exponentially many configurations, yet occupies a vanishing fraction of the full space in the thermodynamic limit. Dynamics from the polarized state, by contrast, occupies a finite fraction of the configuration space, close to anticoncentration and random-state statistics, although chiral symmetry limits this fraction to one third. A weak quasiperiodic field enables the polarized state to occupy half of the configuration space by lifting the constraint imposed by chiral symmetry. The N\'eel state, however, requires a stronger field to reach a comparable anticoncentrated regime. As the field increases further, the occupied fraction decreases for both initial states, revealing a nonmonotonic dependence of Fock-space delocalization on field strength without necessarily implying localization.

nominations.title: Liouvillian spectral snapshots: A reduced-subspace approach for time-dependent and noisy open quantum systems
nominations.authors: Hans Christiansen, Andr\'e Melo, Jens Paaske, Fabrizio Minganti
nominations.abstract: Driven-dissipative quantum devices are routinely operated with time-dependent drives and exposed to temporally correlated classical noise. When these perturbations vary on timescales comparable to the system's intrinsic dynamics, rotating-wave and Markovian approximations can fail, making effective static descriptions unreliable. As a result, accurately modeling systems in this regime often relies on simulating the full time-dependent master equation. This is particularly demanding for processes requiring long integration times, such as rare switching between metastable states, or for stochastic perturbations requiring averaging over many noise realizations. To address these challenges, we introduce Liouvillian spectral snapshots (LSS), a reduced-basis method that enables efficient simulation of such systems by projecting the master equation onto a low-dimensional subspace capturing their coarse-grained dynamics. LSS constructs this subspace by computing the slowly decaying, low-frequency eigenoperators of the Liouvillian at a few adaptively sampled perturbation values and compressing them into a common basis. This basis is built once and can be reused across noise realizations and perturbation parameters, reducing the cost of ensemble averages and parameter sweeps.

nominations.title: Beyond the Kubo formula: unification of adiabatic and isothermal response in quantum systems
nominations.authors: Giuliano Chiriac\`{o}, Vasco Cavina
nominations.abstract: The static limit of the Kubo susceptibility describes the adiabatic response of an isolated quantum system, in which energy-level occupations remain unchanged, and generally differs from the isothermal susceptibility, where these occupations readjust to thermal equilibrium. In this work, we introduce a single dynamical framework in which the adiabatic and isothermal responses arise naturally as two distinct limiting regimes. This can be done by considering explicitly an open system version of the Kubo approach in which the dissipation is governed by a typical thermalization rate of the system. By exchanging the order of the static limit and of the vanishing thermalization rate limit, the protocol yields either the adiabatic or isothermal response. This protocol has a solid physical motivation in terms of the thermalization dynamics and is valid for generic systems. We apply it to the case of the magnetic response of the electron gas and reproduce the expected results.

nominations.title: Witnessing and quantifying stellar rank with the Wigner function
nominations.authors: Oliver Hahn, Alex Maltesson, Varun Upreti, Marike Ellerbroek, Alessandro Ferraro, Saleh Rahimi-Keshari, Ulysse Chabaud, Giulia Ferrini
nominations.abstract: Quantifying non-Gaussianity is essential for assessing the computational power of bosonic quantum systems. We introduce a framework to witness and quantify non-Gaussianity from displaced parity measurements, and we directly apply it to experimental data obtained with superconducting cavities. Our method estimates fidelities with target pure states from the displaced parity measurements, enabling certification of non-Gaussianity via the stellar rank. We further introduce refined witnesses computed by measuring the value of the Wigner function at a few points, providing efficient certification tools outperforming existing ones. Applying these techniques to Fock, binomial, cat, and GKP experimental data, we rigorously certify non-Gaussian resources and establish a stellar rank of $8$ for a GKP state, setting a new benchmark across all quantum platforms. Our methods enable a rigorous quantification of non-Gaussian quantum resources directly applicable to superconducting devices.

nominations.title: Electronic-Structure-Informed Many-Body Encoding for Quantum Machine Learning
nominations.authors: Liangnuo Zhang, Tanner Culpitt, Qiwei Yin, Linghua Zhu, Xiaosong Li
nominations.abstract: Data encoding is a central challenge in quantum machine learning (QML), as it determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states and influences the expressive power and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a physics-informed quantum encoding strategy that exploits the intrinsic many-body structure of electronic systems to establish a direct correspondence between the body order of input descriptors and the locality of quantum gates. Specifically, $n$-body electronic descriptors obtained from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are encoded through $n$-qubit gates, yielding a systematic hierarchy of quantum circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. Using reduced-density-matrix descriptors, we construct quantum machine-learning models incorporating one- through four-body encodings and benchmark their performance in predicting electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces. We demonstrate that increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves prediction accuracy toward the full configuration interaction limit. Remarkably, disconnected many-particle densities constructed from lower-order electronic information achieve accuracy comparable to explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases, providing a computationally inexpensive route to higher-body quantum encodings. These findings establish a connection between the many-body structure of classical data and the design of quantum feature maps, offering a systematic, physically interpretable framework for enhancing the expressivity and predictive performance of quantum machine-learning circuits.

nominations.title: Predictive Maintenance at the Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained with Quantum Optimization
nominations.authors: Filipe Chagas Ferraz
nominations.abstract: This article presents a predictive-maintenance pipeline that detects anomalies in bearings from vibration signals, adapted for deployment at the edge on low-cost microcontrollers, and that uses quantum optimization in two steps of its training. The pipeline consists of a step of vibration feature extraction and a step of classification with a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM). The features are selected by minimum redundancy and maximum relevance (mRMR) with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), under a limit on computing time. The OCSVM is adapted for inference at the edge without floating-point operations and is trained by a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE). In small-scale tests on a simulator, with the Paderborn bearing dataset, the VQE found the optimal selection in 36% of the runs with Adam, and PCE chose better support vectors than chance, until a classical local search made the two equal. A classical baseline, the usual OCSVM trained by SMO with its weights rounded, matched them without any search.

nominations.title: Colloquium: Quantum information processing with ensembles of identical particles
nominations.authors: Matteo Piccolini, Marcin Karczewski, Jin-Shi Xu, Chuan-Feng Li, Guang-Can Guo, Giuseppe Compagno, Farzam Nosrati, Rosario Lo Franco
nominations.abstract: Identical particles underpin most quantum technologies, but the role of indistinguishability in these processes extends far beyond the symmetrization of many-particle states. This Colloquium presents a unified operational perspective on how particle identity, indistinguishability, exchange statistics, and many-particle interference can instead be harnessed as resources for quantum information processing. We first clarify the notions of entanglement and indistinguishability for identical particles, emphasizing their dependence on the accessible measurements and information. We then review how spatial overlap, multiparticle interference, and path identity enable the generation, extraction, protection, and distillation of coherence and entanglement. Their applications to quantum metrology and imaging, state discrimination, teleportation, entanglement swapping, and quantum cloning are examined. Finally, we discuss the thermodynamic role of indistinguishability, from the Gibbs paradox to quantum thermal machines and statistics-driven engines. Across these settings, indistinguishability emerges as a controllable, task-dependent resource whose benefits are determined by state preparation, exchange statistics, interference, and measurement constraints.

nominations.title: Clifford synthesis is NP-complete
nominations.authors: S{\o}ren Fuglede J{\o}rgensen
nominations.abstract: We show that the problem of synthesizing a quantum circuit for a given Clifford operator using at most a specified amount of resources is NP-complete for several resource models of practical interest. Specifically, we study synthesis of a given Clifford operator using single-qubit Clifford gates and two-qubit Clifford gates, with full qubit connectivity and no additional ancilla qubits. With single-qubit gates free and CNOT as the only two-qubit gate, we show that deciding whether a given target admits an implementation using at most a specified number of CNOT gates is NP-complete, and we show that the problem remains NP-complete when any two-qubit Clifford gate is allowed and the budget counts all such gates. Moreover, we show that both results continue to hold when SWAP gates may be inserted for free, and when single-qubit gates are also considered part of the budget. In each case, we build on recent work by Li and Guan and show that there are polynomial-time reductions from Hamiltonian path in grid graphs to these decision problems, using a number of qubits quadratic in the number of grid vertices.

nominations.title: Optical Quantum Memory Processing for Quantum Hashing
nominations.authors: S. A. Moiseev, M. M. Minnegaliev
nominations.abstract: Sender authentication is an important requirement for secure quantum communication networks. We propose programmable photon-echo quantum memory processing of a multi-time-bin photonic qudit for implementing a quantum-hash-based verification protocol. In this approach, using QM, sender (Alice) generates a quantum hash state by transforming a single stored photonic wave packet into the programmable photonic qudit. Bob's memory coherently maps the received time-bin photonic qudit into a single output mode according to phase encoding. Our scheme relies on a time-resolved coherent detection method introduced here, in which the coherent responses from individual time-bins are sequentially accumulated within Bob's spin coherence prior to the final sender verification. The key advantage of this coherent detection for quantum hashing is shown, and its potential applications are also discussed. The performed analysis demonstrates that experimentally verified parameters of contemporary optical quantum memories enable a proof of principle realization of the proposed architecture. These results reveal an additional role for quantum memories, serving not only as synchronization and repeater resources for long-distance quantum communication, but also as active elements for quantum hashing in conventional quantum key distribution systems.

nominations.title: Hypergraph cycle enumeration for efficient inference of planted k-XOR with smooth trade-off
nominations.authors: Arman Babakhani, Enrico Fontana, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Ruslan Shaydulin
nominations.abstract: We introduce hypergraph cycle enumeration (HCE), a simple spectral framework for detecting and recovering planted signals in noisy hypergraph inference problems. We study HCE on one representative problem from this class, namely planted noisy k-XOR, also known as sparse Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). Both theoretically and empirically, HCE achieves comparable recovery behavior to Kikuchi method, matching Kikuchi hierarchy. We identify parameter regimes where HCE outperforms Kikuchi method, showing that neither algorithm is universally better. We also show a subquadratic quantum speedup for HCE by replacing one of the algorithm's steps with a quantum walk. Our classical and quantum algorithms do not refute the quartic quantum speedup of quantum Kikuchi method, which remains valid for the practically relevant regime of large size and high noise strength.

nominations.title: Variational Programs with Open Clocks
nominations.authors: Javaria Ghafoor, Amr Sabry
nominations.abstract: Variational quantum algorithms leave the durations of Hamiltonian evolutions open for a classical optimizer to set. We present VHamilton, a minimal extension of the Hamilton quantum programming language in which such durations are open clocks: one program denotes a family of Hamiltonian trajectories, and a valuation fills its clocks with exact dyadic times, so that each instance is an ordinary Hamilton program that compiles to circuits as before. Because the semantics stays exact and affine in the clocks, the Hamiltonian structure of a variational program remainsavail able for reasoning about every valuation at once. Equivalence becomes a finite calculation, which we mechanize in Agda for a fragment and use to prove the VHamilton form of the compiler rewrite "rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx" for every clock value. We then show what the same structure supports in a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver written in VHamilton and run through a Haskell prototype. It supports a fusion of commuting blocks, a closed form and an expressibility proof for the ansatz, and an exact split of the error between the precision of the target and that of the clocks, with a priori bounds. It also supports a coordinate search whose queries per sweep, fixed by the spectra of the generators, do not grow with the precision. On the benchmark this search reaches the numerically verified optimum of a grid of 134 million valuations in 53 energy queries. It finds the grid optimum in only 21 of 30 validation settings, however, so the gain is conditional, not a global-optimization guarantee.

nominations.title: Preparation of a Laughlin-like fractional Chern insulator on a superconducting quantum processor
nominations.authors: Kamil Dutkiewicz, B\'arbara Andrade, Geza Giedke, Tobias Grass
nominations.abstract: Fractional Chern insulators (FCIs) are lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall states, hosting topological order and fractionalized anyonic excitations. Their realization poses a demanding target for quantum simulation. Here, we realize a bosonic FCI on an IBM Nighthawk superconducting quantum processor using classically optimized variational circuits. We target a Laughlin-like state that is an exact zero-energy ground state of a long-range parent Hamiltonian on a torus, eliminating physical edges and providing a favorable geometry for accessing fractional quantum Hall physics in a small system. On a $4\times4$ qubit lattice, we prepare both the four-boson FCI ground state and a three-boson state hosting two quasiholes. Measurements of particle densities and correlations reproduce the characteristic structure of the target states, while reconstructed chiral magnetization currents resolve the circulating current pattern associated with the quasiholes. The preparation of these strongly correlated topological states with shallow circuits establishes a route toward the digital simulation and manipulation of fractionalized excitations, including measurements of topological invariants and anyonic braiding.

nominations.title: Vacuum amplification across a programmable bosonic Bogoliubov stability boundary in a trapped-ion chain
nominations.authors: Lu Qi, Duanyang Wang, Kenneth R. Brown
nominations.abstract: A quantum oscillator always carries vacuum fluctuations, and modulating its parameters converts them into correlated pairs of real quanta. This vacuum amplification underlies squeezed light and Hawking radiation. In a closed quadratic system, pair creation competes with the energy splitting of the modes, and growth turns exponential only once pairing overcomes the splitting. Here we realize this competition in two motional modes of a trapped-ion chain. A two-mode-squeezing drive creates the pairs, and a beam-splitter coupling splits the motion into two coupled modes at different frequencies. The two rates are tuned and calibrated independently. Starting near the motional ground state, we cross the stability boundary in two ways. First, with the drive at the sum of the two bare-mode frequencies, the phonon number stays bounded until the pairing rate exceeds the splitting and grows exponentially beyond it. Second, tuning the drive into resonance with one coupled mode lowers the threshold to zero, and only that mode is amplified into a squeezed vacuum. Separate control of the two interactions makes the threshold for vacuum amplification programmable. This control can be used to simulate particle creation and quantum phase transitions, and to operate parametrically driven bosonic devices close to their stability limit.

nominations.title: Quantum Vehicle Routing Problem: a smart initialization strategy for ill-conditioned optimization landscapes
nominations.authors: Emanuele Casciaro, Mario De Simone, Stefano Martina, Fabio Mascherpa, Alfonso Amendola, Filippo Caruso
nominations.abstract: With the expansion of complex transport infrastructure, new paths for linking different destinations have emerged, allowing the definition of multiple routes. The introduction of new roads may also lead to disruptions in traffic flow. This problem can be generalized into a special case of VRP, which aims to find the optimal route for a fleet of vehicles within a network of destinations. Finding solutions to this problem requires an exponential number of operations, hindering the ability of exact solvers to deal with large instances, which must therefore be tackled using heuristics, often leading to suboptimal results. Quantum-based algorithms may allow us to find exact solutions in polynomial time with high probability, offering a potential future alternative to classical solvers and in this work, we focus on the QAOA. Our novel contributions are a parameter-initialization strategy that improves the convergence probability and the integration of the subtour constraints directly into the optimization without using additional qubits by employing an approximation of exponential equality constraints. We believe that our results pave the way for effectively solving instances of VRP using quantum-based solutions, leveraging the space-efficient problem encoding and our initialization strategy, which limits the effect of barren-plateau under random parameter initialization.

nominations.title: Entangled Measurement Outcomes for Optimal Postselection in Quantum Batteries
nominations.authors: Yali Du, Zhipei Zhou, Xiaoli Hu
nominations.abstract: Postselection can enhance the performance of a selected quantum battery branch, raising the question of whether the optimum can always be achieved by product measurements on the auxiliary subsystems. For battery auxiliary states obtained by mixing a pure state with global white noise of strength p, the conditional ergotropy reduces to a generalized Rayleigh quotient. For 0<p<1, product postselection attains the joint optimum if and only if the eigenspace associated with the largest generalized eigenvalue contains a product vector. For two auxiliary qubits, a strict product-joint gap therefore occurs precisely when this eigenspace is one dimensional and spanned by an entangled vector. Noisy W and GHZ states display qualitatively different behavior: the three qubit W state exhibits a strict gap throughout 0<p<1, whereas the three qubit GHZ state admits a product optimum. For interacting two qubit batteries, the optimal postselection can switch from a Bell outcome to a product outcome as the coupling strength is varied. By contrast, the outcome averaged capacity and ergotropy are independent of the measurement basis, showing that the joint measurement advantage is genuinely postselective.

nominations.title: Probing Operator Spreading with Local Quantum Fluctuations
nominations.authors: Bert\'{u}lio de Lima Bernardo
nominations.abstract: Measuring out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) is experimentally challenging, often requiring effective reversal of many-body dynamics. Here, we propose an alternative approach to probing operator spreading through local quantum fluctuations, using only forward evolution and local measurements. Motivated by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, we introduce a differential local variance and establish a rigorous bound connecting it to operator noncommutativity. For a ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain in the single-magnon regime, we derive an exact relation between the local variance and a squared-commutator OTOC. In integrable and nonintegrable Ising chains, the differential variance and OTOCs reveal qualitatively consistent propagation fronts. Our results establish local quantum fluctuations as an experimentally accessible, state-dependent, and complementary diagnostic of operator spreading.

nominations.title: FGSM Attack Transferability from Simulation to Quantum Hardware in Network Intrusion Detection
nominations.authors: Zeeshan Ajmal, Kimmo Halunen, Marc Mau{\ss}ner, Volker Reers, Arif Ali Khan
nominations.abstract: Quantum computers are now available through cloud platforms, and recent work has proposed using them to detect network intrusions. It is not yet clear how easily such systems can be attacked. We train a hybrid variational quantum classifier (VQC) on the Friday DDoS subset of CICIDS2017 and test it against two attacks: label flipping during training and FGSM evasion at prediction time. We run the tests in simulation and on IBM hardware, the Fez superconducting processor (Heron r2). We find that two models with similar accuracy can differ greatly in how easily they are attacked. A model that decides with little confidence loses half its detections to a very small change in the input, while a model trained to decide with more confidence needs a much larger change before it fails. Attacks built in simulation against the more confident model also work on real hardware, and the device classifies every unaltered attack sample correctly. Simulated device noise does not reduce accuracy, but it does reduce the model's confidence and makes attacks easier, so accuracy alone does not show how exposed a model is. Label flipping has no measurable effect until 15% of attack labels are changed. These results show that device noise should not be treated as a defense and that reported weaknesses in these classifiers depend partly on how they were trained.

nominations.title: PrivacyFlow: Privacy in AI Agents through Information Flow Analysis and Consequence-Aware Risk Management
nominations.authors: Robin Staab, Tom Wollschl\"ager, Vahab Mirrokni, Reza Shokri
nominations.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents executing multi-step workflows over personal data often misalign with user privacy expectations and leak sensitive, out-of-context information. Although Contextual Integrity (CI) formalizes this problem, existing benchmarks and defenses rarely operationalize CI for realistic multi-step task sequences in evolving environments. In this work, we first introduce agentic PrivacyBench, a benchmark of 5873 tasks in 986 task sequences with dynamic environment updates and CI-grounded allow-sets for sensitive information. We also introduce PrivacyFlow, a defense that separates deliberative privacy planning (System 2) from task execution (System 1), treating each sharing decision as a structured risk-management problem. Before execution, PrivacyFlow traces the provenance and purpose of each planned data flow, models recipient background knowledge, and simulates what external actors could infer. This allows us to model the downstream consequences of disclosure, including inference attacks and context-dependent harms. It then weighs the remaining disclosure risk against task utility and executes a minimized plan, blocks it, or consults the user. Across six models, PrivacyFlow significantly reduces step-level privacy failures and raises the share of completed task sequences without a detected privacy violation by 22--55 percentage points. We further highlight a new privacy--utility--autonomy tradeoff: allowing PrivacyFlow to proactively prompt the user in case of uncertainty can increase authorized task completion at the cost of shifting decision effort back to the user. Our results suggest that proactive CI reasoning can substantially improve agentic privacy and motivate further study of this tradeoff.

nominations.title: Characterizing LLM Agent Behaviors in Module Shadowing Environments
nominations.authors: Shuai Yang, Enmeng Lu, Jinyu Fan, Gongce Cao, Yu Chen, Jiawei Xie, Feifei Zhao, Zhangsheng Wang, Yongyu Jiang, Yi Zeng
nominations.abstract: LLM agents operating in untrusted workspaces face the risk of untrusted code execution during routine tasks, yet final reports and workspace states alone cannot reliably establish whether execution occurred. We introduce an evaluation framework that codes observation, reasoning, execution, and response behaviors from agent trajectories and aligns them with independent environmental records to reconstruct execution histories and verify final reports. We apply this framework to module shadowing, in which a local file is loaded in place of a trusted module during import, enabling untrusted code execution without adversarial prompts. Across 90 trials with 15 models, the payload executed in 51% of direct shadowing trials and 87% of indirect shadowing trials. Even explicit recognition of the shadowing mechanism did not ensure prevention, as the payload ran in 10 of the 29 trials with recorded recognition. These failures were often omitted from final reports, as 49 of the 62 triggered trials ended without mention of the security issue. Three reports even denied execution, including one from a trial in which independent logs recorded 19 payload executions. Final workspace states also obscured prior execution when agents deleted or overwrote the payload marker in 10 triggered trials. These findings demonstrate that combining behavioral coding with independent environmental auditing enables rigorous and transparent evaluation of agent safety.

nominations.title: MetaVul: Agentic Harness Discovery for Vulnerability Detection
nominations.authors: Ira Ceka, Arnav Garg, Ryan Lutz, Ting Zhang, Ratnadira Widyasari, Gail Kaiser, Baishakhi Ray
nominations.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to automate vulnerability detection, but reliable detection is challenging because agents must distinguish subtle, security-relevant fixes from benign code variation. While underlying LLM capability has improved significantly, the accuracy of the agent still depends heavily on the harness: the code that defines the scaffolding around the LLM. Harnesses are typically fixed, and largely hand-written, limiting adaptation to evaluator feedback. Additionally, when harnesses are static, improvements on one dataset or model may not transfer to others. To address these challenges, we introduce MetaVul, a self-improving framework for harness discovery in vulnerability detection. Starting from a seed structured reasoning scaffold, MetaVul uses a workflow-based optimization loop to iteratively refine the harness using feedback from paired vulnerable and patched functions, while preserving the structured reasoning and verdict format. At each iteration, it searches over the history of prior harnesses, with access to their trajectories, logs, and metrics, and it returns a set of Pareto-optimal harnesses. We apply MetaVul to discover agent harnesses for various architectures. A validation set (202 pairs) is used for optimization, while an unseen dataset (430 pairs) is kept as the held-out set. We test whether harnesses learned from one model transfer to others not seen during optimization. Results on both frontier and small LLMs show that the optimized harnesses improve pairwise vulnerability detection up to 23.3 percentage points on the validation set and up to 25.8 points on the held-out set with a Pareto-frontier harness. Harnesses learned with one model also transfer to others. We show that harnesses optimized with one model transfer to another, improving held-out pairwise accuracy by 14.7 points without further optimization.

nominations.title: RiskyPy: Toward Model-Calibrated Prompt Generation for Joint Security and Functionality Evaluation of LLM-Generated Code
nominations.authors: Zacharie Chenail-Larcher, Daniele Lunghi, Melissa Tessa, Quentin Sti\'evenart, Jacques Klein, Tegawend\'e F. Bissyand\'e, Florent Avellaneda, Naouel Moha
nominations.abstract: Evaluating approaches that improve the security of LLM code generation requires datasets that jointly assess security and functionality and remain adapted to the capabilities of the models being studied. However, existing benchmarks are costly to produce and are generally not calibrated to a chosen range of model capabilities. We introduce RiskyPy, an automated pipeline that generates security-oriented code-generation datasets calibrated to model proficiency using functionality and vulnerability canaries. We instantiate RiskyPy for Python using domains covering 18 CWEs from the 2025 CWE Top 25, producing 101 prompts. Experiments on Qwen3-4B and Seed-Coder-8B show that the generated tasks remain functionally accessible, with 57-72% of prompts yielding functional code, while only 5-10% of generations are free of Bandit findings, leaving room for joint evaluation of security and functionality of security improvement approaches.

nominations.title: Prevented is Not Protected: What Attack Success Rate Hides about RAG
nominations.authors: Chahana Dahal, Zuobin Xiong
nominations.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is vulnerable to knowledge poisoning, where adversaries manipulate retrieved evidence to influence model outputs. Existing defenses are primarily evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which obscures defense-induced failures and the mechanisms behind apparent attack prevention. To address this issue, this work introduces \textbf{Aligned RAG Evaluation}, a matched-query protocol that jointly examines clean and poisoned responses, with and without defense. By combining matched conditions analysis, LLM-judge endorsement, and retrieval dependence controls, the proposed framework distinguishes prevented from introduced failures, target mentions from LLM endorsement, and single-passage influence from evidence composition. Experiments on HotpotQA and Natural Questions reveal that existing defenses can introduce unexpected target-positive answers, although they can prevent some attacks, while evaluation criteria can also change defense rankings. Our findings expose critical blind spots in ASR-based evaluation and motivate a more comprehensive assessment of RAG poisoning defenses. The code and the evaluation artifact are available at https://github.com/chxhana/aligned-rag-eval.

nominations.title: CLIC: Closed-Loop Intent Consistency for Securing LLM-Driven Control in Open RAN
nominations.authors: Sunder Ali Khowaja, Kapal Dev, Joongheon Kim, Angelos Antonopoulos, Nikolaos Bartzoudis
nominations.abstract: With the progressive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), researchers are finding ways to integrate them into the control loops of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) to enable slicing and resource management through user intents. However, integration of LLMs in the O-RAN control loop via the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) makes the system vulnerable to \textit{runtime prompt injection threats}, which manipulate control decisions without violating interface authentication, and \textit{residual virtual prompt injection (VPI)} attacks that plant trigger mechanisms to silently steer the behaviour during fine-tuning. Existing studies address only the runtime threat and do not enforce consistency across the full control path, i.e. from the certified A1 intent, through the multi-step LLM trajectory, to the final E2 action. We propose a closed-loop intent-consistency layer (CLIC) that jointly mitigates both threats. The proposed CLIC defines a formal consistency score using a small quantized language model, which is deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification along with a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. We implement CLIC on the OpenAI Cellular (OAIC) platform and evaluate it under domain-adapted JailbreakBench, AdvBench, and VPI workloads. The experimental results show that the proposed CLIC reduces the attack success rate from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, while improving isolation and fairness at slightly higher latency costs, i.e. approximately 27 ms.

nominations.title: Safin-1.5: Safety-Native Architecture and Verifiable Reasoning for Recursive Safety Improvement
nominations.authors: Jingnan Zheng, Cheng Jin, Ming Zhang, Huan Sun, Zhongtian Ma, Kaisen Yang, Ziyuan Zhou, Tong Wu, Dongcheng Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiao Wang, Han Qi, Shu Yu, Ermo Hua, Zongji Yu, Chaozhuo Li, Xiaoyu Wen, Zhekai Chen, Jiawei Zhou, Sirui Chen, Ning Ding, An Zhang, Tat-Seng Chua, Xiangnan He, Xia Hu, Bowen Zhou, Qiaosheng Zhang, Youbang Sun, Xiang Wang, Zhongyu Huang, Chaochao Lu
nominations.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) enables large language models to advance their capabilities through successive updates, but these updates can also introduce new risks and weaken existing safeguards. In line with the AI-45{\deg} Law, we pursue Safety RSI, in which safety develops as an intrinsic capability alongside general model capabilities through continual risk discovery and repair, while preserving utility and limiting over-refusal. We introduce Safin-1.5, a model built on a safety architecture and trained through recursive safety improvement, with an inference-time harness that extends its capabilities to formal reasoning. Our approach comprises three components: i) The safety architecture combines persistent safety states with hazardous-knowledge disentanglement. The former retains and selectively invokes safety knowledge, while the latter relocates targeted hazardous knowledge into removable experts, enabling its removal with minimal impact on general capabilities. ii) Recursive safety improvement establishes a discovery-evaluation-repair loop. The loop identifies new vulnerabilities and uses experimental feedback to develop repair strategies. It accepts updates only when they improve safety while preserving general capabilities and limiting over-refusal. iii) The formal reasoning harness combines the model's language understanding with symbolic inference and verification. Proof-obligation-guided semantic bridging recovers missing relations in formal representations, enabling symbolic solvers to construct checkable proofs under formalized premises and accepted semantic bridges. Experimental results demonstrate that Safin-1.5 achieves safety and reasoning performance, outperforming frontier models.

nominations.title: "Shall We Approve?" Consequence-Aware Approval for Autonomous Coding Agents
nominations.authors: Weiheng Wu, Junkai Chen, Zhensu Sun, Jieke Shi, Yunbo Lyu, David Lo
nominations.abstract: Coding agents increasingly rely on automated approvers to decide whether a proposed shell command may run. Existing approvers, from rule-based checkers to guardrail models and deployed permission classifiers, base their decisions on the text of the request and command. Yet a command's behavior depends on the code it invokes and the state of the workspace, and systems that observe file changes leave the assessment to the agent or a human after execution. We present Caper, a consequence-aware approval mechanism that pre-executes each command in a snapshotted sandbox, provides an independent approver with a bounded report of its observed effects, commits allowed commands, and rolls back blocked ones with a reason the agent can act on. Compared with six existing systems, Caper achieves the lowest harmful-outcome rate on SABER (6.7% versus at least 14.8%) and YoloFS-Ext, a benchmark we build in which harmful behavior is hidden inside invoked tools (7.8% versus at least 35.3%), while blocking 1.0% of the safe twins of the dangerous tasks in YoloFS-Ext.

nominations.title: LiHA: Worse is Better for Lightweight Hash-based Source Authentication
nominations.authors: Negin Dehghanchaleshtori, Homit Dalia, Himanshu Chandra, Rohan Tripathi, Marc E. Fiuczynski, Richard P. Martin
nominations.abstract: The omission of source IP authentication remains a fundamental vulnerability in the Internet. Existing approaches rely on routing plausibility, topology assumptions, per-flow state, or wide deployment. These requirements have kept strong source authentication out of the data plane. As simplicity is the key to deployability, we present LiHA, a lightweight source authentication mechanism built around operations that routers already perform efficiently. LiHA binds secret keys to source prefixes using longest prefix match and authenticates each packet with a single message authentication code (MAC). The data plane requires no handshakes, per-flow state, or per-packet control plane access. A sender performs one prefix lookup and one fixed-size hash. The verifier repeats the same operations and forwards the packet only if the MAC matches. LiHA is designed for incremental deployment. It primarily protects against off-path attackers that spoof source prefixes they do not control. An on-path attacker can replay valid authenticated packets until the key rotates. LiHA does not eliminate every denial-of-service threat. Instead, it confines accepted traffic to authenticated source prefix space within participating networks. We argue that simpler source authentication with clear limits is more likely to be deployed. We implemented LiHA in three environments: as a set of user-space libraries, as eBPF programs, and in an FPGA. We found that the user-space implementation had very high overheads. The eBPF implementation got reasonable single thread performance even with a software based cryptographic hash. We found that only the FPGA could obtain 100 Gbps single thread performance, but that was only when bypassing the kernel using a DPDK user-level networking stack.

nominations.title: Does Showing Agents the Privilege of Their Tools Reduce Over-Privileged Tool Selection?
nominations.authors: Simon Parkinson, Mauro Vallati, Zhipeng Wang, Mustafa Mustafa
nominations.abstract: When several tools can complete a task, an agent that picks the most powerful one holds more authority than the task needs. Recent work demonstrates that language-model agents do this often, and more so after a tool fails. Approaches to restrict focus so far on either enforcing least privilege outside the model or retraining the model. We ask a simpler question: does it help to tell the agent what each tool's privilege is? To investigate this question, we run all 544 ToolPrivBench scenarios on eight models, three run locally, and five through a hosted API, under five conditions: (1) no signal, (2) a least-privilege instruction, (3) privilege class and cost shown in each tool description, (4) both the instruction and privilege information, and (5) a matched neutral-metadata control. Showing privilege lowers premature escalation on every model that over-privileges at a measurable rate, reducing over-privileged selection by up to 19.3 percentage points (50\%), whereas irrelevant metadata in the same format does not. On most models, however, information alone mainly delays escalation until the standard tools have been tried. Combined with the instruction it more often avoids escalation, and the share of scenarios completed without a risk tool rises on seven of the eight models, reaching 51.1\% safe completion from a baseline of 18.8\% on the strongest-performing configuration. Visible privilege is therefore a cheap complement to enforcement rather than a substitute.

nominations.title: Towards Elastic Least Privilege for Agent Planning
nominations.authors: Simon Parkinson, Zhipeng Wang, Mustafa Mustafa
nominations.abstract: General-purpose AI agents require authority that changes between tasks and during execution. Common deployments trade broad permissions that expose unnecessary authority and narrow permissions that raise approval requests. Existing mechanisms can enforce dynamic authority, but agent tool interfaces rarely provide the agent's planner, the component that chooses its actions, a means of comparing the authority required by alternative actions or of seeing the cost of the authority it already holds. Drawing on the rich history of access control research, we propose the concept of \emph{elastic least privilege}, in which an agent begins with a small baseline of authority and may acquire more within an owner-defined envelope. Elevations are leased and measured against a replenishing budget. Their cost increases with power, proximity to mandatory safety invariants, and repeated requests. Costs are visible to the planner, which can prefer lower-privilege choices and release authority it no longer needs. Authority returns automatically to the baseline when a lease expires, when it is released, or when the budget is exhausted, while persistent legitimate demand may prompt an owner-approved change to the baseline. Building on prior risk-priced and budget-aware access control, we redesign these mechanisms for agents. How best to implement the approach and how well it works in practice are open research questions. In this paper, we present how the approach could work, illustrate the model, and set an open research agenda.

nominations.title: Adaptive Dynamic Security for Operational Technology Against AI-Powered Attacks
nominations.authors: Mohamed Chahine Ghanem
nominations.abstract: Operational technology now faces attackers whose tempo is set by AI. We present ADS-OT, an adaptive dynamic security framework modelling defensive posture as a partially observable decision problem. A reinforcement-learning policy adapts monitoring, access, deception, and segmentation under a safety-governance layer, reducing attack-path completion, detection, and containment versus static baselines.

nominations.title: An Incentive-Aligned Trust-Centric Coordination Layer for Heterogeneous Blockchain Interoperability
nominations.authors: Saeed Moradi, Sara Rouhani
nominations.abstract: The interoperability between permissioned and public blockchains is hampered by asymmetric privacy, trust, and governance assumptions. We propose a coordination architecture that decouples cross-domain trust management and privacy enforcement from underlying blockchain protocols, requiring no protocol-level modifications. The framework integrates cryptographic unlinkability mechanisms with incentive-compatible relay selection, combining stake-weighted participation and temporally accumulated reputation to align economic commitment with sustained correctness. We formalize the adversarial model and derive security and privacy properties for cross-domain coordination, demonstrating robustness against Sybil infiltration, collusion, and strategic stake concentration. Simulation-based analysis characterizes key design trade-offs between quorum thresholds, reputation memory, and anonymity parameters, indicating that privacy-preserving coordination can be achieved without degrading responsiveness or incentive stability when parameters are properly tuned.

nominations.title: Closing the Applied Cybersecurity Gap in Critical Infrastructure: A Cyber-to-Physical Security Assessment Framework for Water Systems
nominations.authors: Halil Dursunoglu, Kaan Sulkalar
nominations.abstract: The integration of information technology and operational technology in water infrastructure creates pathways through which cyber compromise may affect physical service delivery. This study revisits the Applied Cybersecurity Gap (ACG) framework by evaluating an experimental Applied Cybersecurity Gap Index (ACGI) alongside the Cyber-to-Physical Propagation Rate (CPPR), defined as the proportion of initially compromised trials that produce a specified physical-impact outcome. The expanded evaluation comprises 2,160 synthetic trials across three water-network benchmarks, including EPANET Example Network 3 (Net3), and couples declared cyber-attack progression rules with hydraulic simulations. A source-trained machine-learning model evaluated on 247 compromised Net3 trials achieved ROC-AUC 0.772, PR-AUC 0.775, and F1 0.733, compared with 0.661, 0.642, and 0.704 for a scenario-only baseline. The configuration-cluster bootstrap interval for the ROC-AUC difference was 0.038--0.183. A separate 720-run Net3 hydraulic operating-point sensitivity analysis achieved the study's exploratory baseline pressure criterion in all reruns, preserved 717 of 720 physical-impact labels, and produced ROC-AUC 0.791 with the frozen source-trained model. Additional analyses examine the sensitivity of CPPR to the physical-impact threshold and assumed control-blocking probabilities, and demonstrate that the ACGI--CPPR association is partly induced by the simulation design rather than independently validated. The findings establish a reproducible simulation-based assessment workflow, but do not constitute field calibration of cybersecurity-control effectiveness or prediction of real-world utility incidents.

nominations.title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents
nominations.authors: Runze Zhao, Dongruo Zhou, Sumit Kumar Jha, Nathaniel D. Bastian, Ankit Shah
nominations.abstract: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.

nominations.title: Evaluating Structural and SAT Attack Resilience in Cryptographic Dynamic Logic Locking via Keystream Capping
nominations.authors: Nahush Tambe, Naseeruddin Lodge, Vineet Chadalavada, Fareena Saqib
nominations.abstract: Untrusted third-party entities throughout the semiconductor supply chain expose proprietary hardware intellectual property to reverse engineering, piracy, and overproduction. While logic locking counters this threat by embedding key-dependent logic, conventional static key-gates remain vulnerable to both oracle-guided SAT attacks and structural removal attacks due to their time-invariant netlist signatures. Dynamic schemes such as STREAMLOCK mitigate oracle attacks by continuously masking signals with cryptographic keystream, achieving near 50\% Hamming distance output corruption under incorrect keys with low hardware overhead. However, confining key-gates to primary outputs leaves internal combinational cones vulnerable to single-tap structural bypasses. This work extends dynamic logic locking by distributing key-gates within internal paths prioritized via fault-propagation analysis. The original and internally-hardened architectures are evaluated against structural removal attacks and a bounded, unrolling-based SAT-style attack across three ISCAS'85 benchmarks. Distributing masking internally raises the uninformed attacker's brute-force search space from 6 candidate node subsets to over $10^{45}$ for the largest benchmark. Crucially, empirical analysis reveals that topological relocation alone does not prevent algebraic key extraction when wide circuits expose numerous keystream bits per clock cycle. To eliminate this leak, a keystream-bit reuse cap is introduced to restrict per-cycle exposure independent of circuit width. Under this constraint, SAT-solver tractability encounters an immediate computational cliff, transitioning sharply from rapid under-constrained solving to timeout thresholds without disclosing the secret key. Integrating fault-aware internal placement with keystream reuse capping delivers joint resilience against structural bypasses and bounded SAT attacks.

nominations.title: Who Swept My ETH? Uncovering EIP-7702-Based Ether Redirection Attacks on Ethereum
nominations.authors: Ziwei Li, Tianwei Chen, Jiajing Wu, Zigui Jiang, Yuhong Nan, Yaobo Huang, Bowen Song, Zibin Zheng
nominations.abstract: EIP-7702 introduces a new transaction type that allows Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) on major EVM-compatible chains to delegate execution to arbitrary contract codes temporarily. While enhancing functionality, this mechanism facilitates a novel threat: the \underline{E}IP-7702-Based \underline{E}ther \underline{R}edirection \underline{A}ttack (EERA). In such an attack, a victim is delegated to a malicious sweeper contract, which automatically redirects incoming ETH transfers to an address controlled by the attacker. As a nascent attack paradigm arising from protocol evolution, the underlying mechanisms and security implications of EERA remain systematically unexplored. To bridge this gap, we provide the first formal analysis of the EERA attack model and propose SweeperHunter, a framework that detects these attacks through transaction analysis. By evaluating transactions from the first ten months following the introduction of EIP-7702 on Ethereum mainnet, we have identified 4,668,209 malicious delegations, 20,443 attack transactions and 508 ETH sweeper contracts, forming the first EERA dataset. Finally, we analyze this attack from both attacker and victim perspectives, derive key insights, and propose corresponding mitigation strategies. We reveal the prevalence of EERA, as approximately 70\% of the observed delegations point toward ETH sweeper contracts. Furthermore, we observe a notable lack of effective responses from victims; specifically, over 600,000 accounts failed to revoke or update their malicious delegations promptly, thereby remaining in a state of vulnerability. Our research is expected to facilitate understanding and mitigation of this emerging threat posed by EIP-7702.

nominations.title: PP-Mark: Provable and Publicly Verifiable Watermarking for Generative AI
nominations.authors: Hankyeong Ko, Taehoon Kim
nominations.abstract: Generative AI models now produce images indistinguishable from real data, making publicly verifiable provenance essential; however, existing watermarking methods become vulnerable to forgeries and adversarial optimization attacks once their detectors are made public. We propose PP-Mark, a provenance framework that anchors lightweight statistical detection to a zero-knowledge proof of the embedding process, ensuring that forged content cannot pass full verification by construction. We establish formal unforgeability under standard cryptographic assumptions and validate PP-Mark against representative baselines across two latent-diffusion models (SD2.1 and SDXL), demonstrating resistance to black-box imprint forgery, white-box optimization, and regeneration attacks while remaining practical for decentralized verification. Code is available at https://github.com/hko920920/PP-Mark_NeurIPS2026

nominations.title: AgentShield: Fortifying Web Applications Against AI Agents and Agentic Browsers
nominations.authors: Moiz Ali, Nafis Karim, Rownak Islam, Jyotirmay Chauhan, Dhruv Kuchhal, Jason Polakis
nominations.abstract: LLM-powered browser agents are transforming web automation by autonomously interacting with websites and executing complex workflows. However, the effectiveness of existing anti-bot defenses against these systems remains unclear. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of modern agentic browsers against widely deployed anti-bot mechanisms, characterizing their capabilities, limitations, and behavioral differences from humans. Our results show that many defenses designed for traditional automation struggle to reliably detect autonomous AI-driven agents. Accordingly, we introduce AgentShield, a behavioral fingerprinting framework that targets the Perception-Reasoning-Action (PRA) loop underlying agentic user clients. By leveraging dynamic web forms that progressively reveal content and capture fine-grained interaction telemetry, AgentShield exposes behavioral artifacts that enable differentiation between human users and autonomous agents. We further demonstrate Extinction-induced Policy Drift (EPD), a novel attack in which repeated obstruction of task completion causes agents to relax their safeguards and engage in unsafe behaviors. Finally, we present defensive prompt injection techniques that exploit agent-specific weaknesses to mitigate emerging forms of autonomous web abuse that rely on content extraction. Our results highlight both the shortcomings of current web defenses against agentic user clients and the feasibility of practical detection mechanisms tailored to this new generation of web automation.
